meaning: 'Born of the Jewel' — the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family

phonemes.desc: Flapped r and unaspirated dental t: ratna, 'jewel, gift' — the first half of the name, quick and light.
Plain dental n with short a; the word for jewel closed and ready to compound.
s with anusvāra m: the prefix sam-, 'together, fully' — intensification before the root.
Aspirated voiced bh [bʱ], breathy and warm, from the root √bhū, 'to become, to arise'.
Labial approximant v with short a; sambhava, 'arising, origin' — the name's resolution.

pronunciation.approximation: 'ruht-nuh-SUHM-bhuh-vuh' — five even syllables, no hard stress; aim the breathy 'bh' in the middle of the word.

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: ratna 'jewel, gift' — as in the Three Jewels (triratna) and the Ratnakūṭa collection of Mahāyāna sūtras

kin.label: Sanskrit
kin.form: sambhava 'arising, origin', from sam- 'together' + √bhū 'to become' — the same root that yields English 'be' via *bheuə-

kin.label: Tibetan
kin.form: Rin chen 'byung, 'Born of Jewel', the name by which Tibetan Buddhism knows him; Japanese Esoteric Buddhism calls him Hōshō Nyorai 宝生如来, 'Jewel-Arising Tathāgata'

pronunciation.note: Ratnasambhava is Tier 2 by the mechanical rule: the normalized Sanskrit form uses plain ASCII letters — no diacritic or distinctive atomic letter distinguishes it from the ASCII input. The scholarship lives in the compound itself: ratna 'jewel' + sambhava 'born', the title of the Dhyānibuddha of the southern jewel family.

domains.title: Ratnasambhava
domains.subtitle: Jewel-Born
domains.lead: Ratnasambhava is the Dhyānibuddha of the southern quarter, the 'Born of the Jewel' whose open palm bestows the treasures of the Buddhist path. Head of the ratna, jewel family, he transmutes pride and avarice into the wisdom of equality — the insight that all beings, like all gems, share one nature.

cards.name: Born of the Jewel
cards.desc: ratna 'jewel' + sambhava 'arising': the name is a theology — awakening as something precious and self-generated, born from within.

cards.name: The Southern Quarter
cards.desc: He presides over the south, the direction of summer's ripening; his color is gold, his element earth, his mood abundance.

cards.name: The Gift-Bestowing Hand
cards.desc: His mudrā is varada, the open palm of giving — generosity (dāna) is the first perfection and the gate of his jewel family.

cards.name: Unicode Restoration
cards.desc: Preserved as a flagship temple: the plain-ASCII name claims the jewel-born Buddha of the south for the Unicode web.

symbols.name: The wish-fulfilling jewel (cintāmaṇi)
symbols.meaning: The ratna that grants every need — his family's emblem and the 'jewel' from which he is born.

symbols.name: Gold and ochre
symbols.meaning: His body-color: the southern light of ripening crops, wealth, and generosity made visible.

symbols.name: The varada mudrā
symbols.meaning: Palm turned outward at the knee — the gesture of giving that unties the knot of miserliness and pride.

symbols.name: The horse
symbols.meaning: His vāhana or throne-mount — as Akṣobhya has the elephant and Amitābha the peacock, the south rides on energy.

symbols.name: Māmakī, his consort
symbols.meaning: In the five-family maṇḍala his consort is Māmakī, the stainless one — wisdom of equality in female form.

mythology.lead: Ratnasambhava has no biography of battles and loves; as a Dhyānibuddha his 'mythology' is a maṇḍala — a cosmic arrangement in which the south, the color gold, the gesture of giving, and the wisdom of equality converge on a single figure born of the wish-fulfilling jewel.

myths.title: Born of the Jewel in Akaniṣṭha
myths.text:
In the Mahāyāna cosmology codified in the yoga-tantra canon — above all the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, the 'Compendium of the Truth of All Tathāgatas' — each of the five Dhyani Buddhas began as a bodhisattva who made universal vows before the Buddhas of former eons and attained perfect enlightenment in Akaniṣṭha, the highest heaven of form. Ratnasambhava's vow was the vow of giving: to ripen in all beings the capacity for generosity, the first of the perfections (pāramitā), until they too stood as self-arisen jewels. When the vow was complete, he awoke as the Buddha of the south, and the other Buddhas assigned him the ratna family — the line of beings whose affliction is avarice and whose fruit is equality.

The 'myth' is doctrine wearing narrative dress: enlightenment here is not escape from the world but its enrichment — a Buddha whose very title declares that what is most precious arises from within.

myths.title: The South Gate of the Five Families
myths.text:
The five-family maṇḍala arranges the awakened mind as a cosmic cross: Vairocana at the center, Akṣobhya in the east, Ratnasambhava in the south, Amitābha in the west, Amoghasiddhi in the north. Each presides over a family (kula) of beings bound by one of the five poisons and liberated by its counter-wisdom. Ratnasambhava's family is the ratna-kula: those in whom pride and greed dominate. His counter-agent is the wisdom of equality (samatā-jñāna) — the direct seeing that self and other, gold and dust, are equal in emptiness — and his emblematic act is the varada mudrā, the open hand. The Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha and its commentarial tradition assign him his mantra, his color, and his throne; Tibetan manuals such as those of the Sa skya school describe his visualization in detail for initiates.

The maṇḍala's teaching is exact: the poison of the south is not destroyed but converted — avarice, rightly seen, is the very energy of giving.

myths.title: Māmakī and the Wisdom of Equality
myths.text:
In the later tantric development of the five-Buddha system, each Dhyani Buddha is paired with a consort who embodies the wisdom (prajñā) complementing his method (upāya): Ākāśadhātvīśvarī with Vairocana, Locanā with Akṣobhya, Māmakī with Ratnasambhava, Pāṇḍaravāsinī with Amitābha, Tārā with Amoghasiddhi. Māmakī — 'the Stainless One', golden in color, her name a cult-title already known from the inscriptions and art of the Gupta age — stands at the south gate of the maṇḍala as the wisdom of equality in female form. In Tibetan iconography the pair appears in yab-yum, the divine embrace: two figures, one awakening. Snellgrove and other historians of Indo-Tibetan Buddhism trace this pairing through the yoga-tantra commentaries into the initiatory maṇḍalas still conferred in Tibetan lineages today.

The pairing is the theology of relationship: equality is not a solitary insight but one that arrives, as wisdom does, between two.

myths.title: From Nālandā to the Roof of the World
myths.text:
The historical career of Ratnasambhava's image runs along the monastic highways of medieval Asia. In the Pala-period east (8th–12th centuries), the great universities of Nālandā and Vikramaśīla taught the yoga-tantras in which the five-Buddha maṇḍala is codified, and their bronze workshops cast small gilt images for the caravan routes north. With the first wave of Buddhism's entry into Tibet — the invited scholars of the late 8th century, the founding of bSam yas — the southern Buddha crossed the Himalaya and received his Tibetan name, Rin chen 'byung. The Newars of the Kathmandu Valley absorbed the five Buddhas so completely that every stūpa carries a gilt pañca-dhyāni set at its crown, Ratnasambhava facing south. Eastward, the Tang esoteric masters rendered him as Baosheng Rulai and transmitted his maṇḍala to Japan, where the Shingon school enshrines him as Hōshō Nyorai in the Womb-Realm maṇḍala of Tō-ji and Mount Kōya.

No single event canonized him; a thousand caravans did. His afterlife is a map of the routes Buddhism itself travelled.

lore.syncretism: In China the Tang esoteric masters rendered him as Baosheng Rulai 寶生如來, 'Jewel-Arising Tathāgata', and his southern court survives in both Womb- and Diamond-Realm maṇḍalas transmitted to Japan, where Shingon knows him as Hōshō Nyorai. In Tibet he is Rin chen 'byung, central to the initiation maṇḍalas of all four classes of tantra. The Newars of the Kathmandu Valley absorbed the five Buddhas so completely that every stūpa carries his gilt image facing south — Buddhist architecture turned into a permanent five-direction liturgy. In the modern West he has been reinterpreted through Jungian psychology, the gold of the south read as the individuated self — a reading that tells us more about the interpreters than about the maṇḍala, but which keeps his image circulating far beyond any monastery.
lore.culturalLegacy: Ratnasambhava's cult never had a single great pilgrimage centre; it lives wherever the five-Buddha maṇḍala is painted — on the toranas of Nepalese stūpas, in the assembly halls of Ladakhi and Tibetan monasteries, in the Tang maṇḍalas preserved at Tō-ji and the thousand-year rites of Mount Kōya. His gift-gesture made him a patron of abundance, addressed by farmers and merchants alike. In contemporary Buddhist practice, meditations on his golden light and equality-wisdom are taught in Tibetan lineages, while museums from the Met to the British Museum display the Pala-period bronzes through which his image once travelled the monastic world. In Southeast Asia the five-Buddha scheme crowns the stūpas of the old Khmer and Javanese empires, so that Borobudur itself is, among other things, a monument to the jewel-born Buddha of the south.
lore.extendedMeditation: Ratnasambhava is the Buddha who asks what wealth is for. Born of the jewel, he does not hoard it: his hand is open, palm outward — the only mudrā among the five Dhyani Buddhas that gives rather than reassures, subdues, meditates, or protects. His teaching is that avarice is equality denied: the delusion that my gem and yours are rival claims on a finite world. To meditate on the south-facing Buddha is to imagine a richness that increases precisely by being given away. In an age built on scarcity mechanics and attention economies, the jewel-born one is quietly heretical: he promises that the wish-fulfilling gem was never a commodity, and that the hand which opens is itself the treasure.
lore.archaeology: The five-Dhyani-Buddha scheme is stamped across medieval Asian sacred geography. At Borobudur in Java (8th–9th century) the galleries distribute the five Buddhas with their characteristic mudrās. In the western Himalaya, the 11th-century temples of Alchi and Tabo preserve five-Buddha wall cycles in which the southern, golden figure displays the gift-bestowing hand. Pala-period (8th–12th century) bronze workshops of the Nālandā region exported small gilt images of the southern Buddha along the monastic routes into Tibet, and Newar craftsmen made the gilt-copper pañca-dhyāni set a fixture of every Kathmandu Valley stūpa — the crowning faces of Swayambhū and Boudhanath still include him. Tang and Japanese maṇḍala paintings preserved at Tō-ji, Shōgo-in, and the repositories of Mount Kōya fix his iconography in silk.
